report:
Conclusion: the claim is **plausible but not proven for stroke specifically**. The strongest evidence supports olive oil as part of a Mediterranean-style diet lowering overall cardiovascular events; evidence that olive oil alone reduces stroke is weaker and inconsistent.

The best randomized evidence is PREDIMED: high-risk adults assigned to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts had fewer major cardiovascular events than a reduced-fat control group; the trial was retracted and republished after randomization problems, with broadly similar conclusions (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1800389; https://www.bmj.com/content/364/bmj.l341). But it tested a dietary pattern plus olive oil/nuts, so it cannot isolate olive oil or stroke alone.

Observational evidence is supportive for cardiovascular disease and mortality, though confounding is likely because olive-oil users often have healthier diets/lifestyles (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623257/). Importantly, a large U.S. analysis reported lower CVD/CHD risk when olive oil replaced butter/margarine/mayonnaise, but **no significant effect on stroke** (https://www.heart.org/en/news/2020/03/05/olive-oil-may-lower-heart-disease-risk).

Practical takeaway: replacing saturated fats with extra-virgin olive oil within a Mediterranean pattern is reasonable and may lower cardiovascular risk; simply adding olive oil calories is not established to prevent stroke.
